content:
Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and the more recent cheap non-designer option both sell themselves on built-in AI, but in early July, the company announced a "ridiculous" limit on free uses of an accessibility feature.

In effect, Meta retrofitted a paywall to a hardware product already sold to customers. Update: the social media company now says it will "pause" plans to add a paywall to this feature – see at the end of this post.

Meta first began rolling out Conversation Focus in December last year.

It's a clever application of AI, and one of its biggest strengths is that it uses on-device processing, so neither privacy nor cellular data are sacrificed.

However, Meta is now imposing a limit on how many times users can use this feature without paying extra, according to The Verge.

This is especially unacceptable. First, as The Verge's Sean Hollister points out, the feature runs on-device and does not use Meta's servers, so there is no reasonable justification for charging users. Second, this is an accessibility feature, and some users may have purchased the glasses precisely for this reason.

Top comment by KJ705

It's hard to imagine paywalling an accessibility feature will be received well in the long run.

Accessibility feature share: I recently bought my mum a pair of AirPods Pro 3 specifically to use as hearing aids. I was very impressed with the hearing aid functionality but wish it did a better job of cutting down background noise. She found it extremely useful.

When The Verge reached out to Meta for comment, the company replied that the limit "currently" applies only to Conversation Focus, implying that other AI features may also be subject to usage caps in the future. Meta told us that because this feature is designed for people with normal hearing, they do not regard it as an accessibility feature. But I think that's just a matter of semantics, since some people do find it harder than others to follow conversations in noisy environments.

All of this may be good news for the upcoming Apple Glasses – even if their initial price tag is expected to be higher, it gives consumers one more reason to choose a company with a better reputation when buying their AI smart glasses. The company has consistently said that it never requires accessibility features to deliver a return on investment, viewing them instead as a way to contribute to a better world.

Apple Glasses are expected to launch sometime next year.

Update: Meta told The Verge it has paused the plan to limit uses of Conversation Focus, but has not given up on the idea of putting some of its glasses' features behind a paywall.
